title: Legal tasks: Work maps do not prove automation
desc: Catalogues analytical, documentary, interpersonal and administrative activities without establishing capability, adoption or autonomous readiness.

kps.k: This cluster maps work at task level; it does not establish AI capability, adoption or job displacement.
kps.d: The supplied Frontier AI excerpts describe benchmark composition, OpenAI Signals supplies a work-activity catalogue, and Briggs and Kodnani illustrate potential AI applications. Their distinct contribution is to specify activities that researchers can classify or test, rather than demonstrate that AI performs whole legal roles. The excerpts contain no substantive disagreement or comparative performance findings.

kps.k: The benchmark emphasises business analysis and advice, with legal work embedded in a broader business-task mix.
kps.d: Frontier AI reports 117 intermediate-level questions on business or financial data analysis, 88 on business or operational advice, 48 on evaluating programs, practices or processes, and 44 on business or financial risks. It also includes legal research, regulatory-impact analysis, compliance review, negotiation and document preparation. These counts describe coverage, not success rates or the occupational prevalence of those activities; intermediate and detailed classifications should not be treated as separate capability findings.

kps.k: The activity catalogues distinguish document and analytical work from interpersonal, supervisory and administrative legal work.
kps.d: OpenAI Signals separates research, decisions, drafting and recordkeeping from advice, client discussions, presentation in proceedings, mediation, negotiation and direction of legal activities. Its wider catalogue also includes physical work outside legal services. This breadth describes a classification system, not tasks users necessarily perform with ChatGPT. Its data-quality and compliance checks likewise do not specifically denote human verification of AI output.

kps.k: Potential applications extend beyond drafting, but illustrative complexity does not establish readiness for autonomous work.
kps.d: Briggs and Kodnani describe compliance review and arguments in ambiguous cases, data analysis and forecasting, updates to reports and models, and scheduling with task assignment and completion-time estimates. Their examples span simple form checks through complicated court motions. These illustrations do not demonstrate independent judicial capability, reliable forecasting or successful deployment. The practical implication for interpreting this cluster is to match any subsequent capability or adoption evidence to the specific task and context, rather than infer automation of an occupation from its inclusion in a table.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by presenting a task-level map of benchmark composition rather than evidence of automation. It classifies questions using intermediate and detailed O*NET work activities and orders them by question count; these counts indicate what the benchmark covers, not how well AI performs, whether organisations have adopted it, or whether whole legal roles are ready for autonomous execution. Its main contribution is to show that legal and regulatory activities—including legal research, regulatory-impact analysis, contract negotiation and document preparation—sit within a broader benchmark weighted toward business analysis, operational advice and process evaluation. The material variation is therefore within task coverage, spanning analytical, operational and legal activities and two classification levels, rather than disagreement with the proposition. Because the evidence comes from one curated research source, this assessment should not be generalised to academia or research voices overall.

The legal-tech-vendor evidence supports the proposition in a limited, descriptive sense. OpenAI Signals supplies a granular work-activity taxonomy that separates legal research and regulatory analysis from drafting, recordkeeping, client interaction, proceedings, negotiation, supervision and administration. That task-level differentiation is consistent with the proposition that work maps identify activities rather than establish automation of an entire legal role. Materially, however, the source provides no capability scores, adoption measurements, deployment evidence, causal findings or job-displacement estimates. Its legal categories also sit within a much broader cross-occupational catalogue, reinforcing that inclusion is classification rather than proof that ChatGPT performs the activity. There is no substantive internal disagreement in the supplied vendor evidence; the main variation is between analytical and documentary tasks on one hand and interpersonal or supervisory tasks on the other. Because the curated evidence contains only this source, it cannot establish how prevalent this position is among legal-tech vendors generally.

The selected market-analyst source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Briggs and Kodnani catalogue potential AI applications at the task level—covering compliance review, ambiguous-case reasoning, data analysis and forecasting, knowledge updating, scheduling and task assignment—without presenting evidence of actual performance, deployment, autonomous readiness or job displacement. The main variation is in the complexity of the illustrations, which range from checking forms to ruling on a complicated court motion. That breadth maps possible applications but does not show that AI can reliably or independently perform the more complex work. Because this professional-voice category contains only one supplied source, no broader consensus or prevalence among market analysts, consultancies and the press can be inferred.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source supports the proposition that task catalogues do not by themselves prove automation. Briggs and Kodnani map potential AI applications across compliance review, ambiguous-case reasoning, data analysis, forecasting, knowledge updating, scheduling and task assignment. The examples range from routine form checks to ruling on a complicated court motion, but the source supplies no empirical performance results, adoption evidence, reliability findings or evidence that AI can autonomously perform whole legal roles. The principal reason for support is therefore evidentiary: listing a task as a potential application identifies something that might be tested or assisted, not demonstrated capability or occupational displacement. Internal variation lies mainly in task type and complexity—documentary and analytical activities sit alongside coordination work, while simple and highly consequential examples appear in the same illustrative framework. That breadth reinforces the need for task- and context-specific capability evidence rather than weakening the proposition. Because only one source is supplied for this period, this assessment characterises that source alone and does not establish the prevalence of this view among 2023–2024 publications.

The 2026 sources support the proposition that task and benchmark maps identify categories of work but do not, by themselves, prove AI capability, adoption, autonomous readiness or job displacement. Their common basis is evidentiary restraint: both materials classify activities rather than report performance or deployment outcomes. There is material variation in what they map. OpenAI Signals provides a broad, cross-occupational taxonomy that separates legal research, drafting and recordkeeping from client interaction, proceedings, negotiation, supervision and administration. The Frontier AI benchmark instead reports the composition and question counts of a business-oriented test set in which legal and regulatory tasks are embedded. Thus, one source supplies a general activity architecture while the other defines benchmark coverage; neither establishes that AI can reliably perform the listed tasks or automate whole legal roles. Because these are curated sources, their agreement should not be treated as evidence of how prevalent this view is among 2026 publications.
